name: GCSE Economics (AQA 8136)
material_vintage: AQA GCSE Economics (8136) specification, for first teaching from September 2017, linked from aqa.org.uk/8136 and itemised on 2026-09-27: all 11 topics across the two papers -- Paper 1 'How markets work' (Topics 1-6: Economic foundations; Resource allocation; How prices are determined; Production, costs, revenue and profit; Competitive and concentrated markets; Market failure) and Paper 2 'How the economy works' (Topics 7-11: Introduction to the national economy; Government objectives; How the government manages the economy; International trade and the global economy; The role of money and financial markets), plus the quantitative skills requirement running through both papers (at least 10% of total marks). Assessment: two linear written papers, each 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks, 50% of the GCSE -- each paper's Section A is 10 multiple-choice questions plus a range of calculation, short and extended-response questions, and Section B is five questions mixing calculations, short and extended responses. Stage tests and the mock are original questions in AQA's style, never real past-paper items; every numerical worked example (elasticities, costs/revenue/profit, economies of scale, gross/net pay, GDP/CPI/unemployment-rate calculations, balance of payments, exchange rates, interest) was computed and verified when this course was built.
level_source: RQF Level 2 (GCSE, grades 1-9), per Ofqual's Register of Regulated Qualifications listing for this specification

learner_notices.text: AQA GCSE Economics relies heavily on diagrams (demand/supply curves, shifts, externality diagrams). This course describes every diagram precisely in words (axes, curve shapes, direction and cause of any shift); sketch each one by hand as it is described, since being able to draw and label these diagrams accurately is itself examined.

At least 10% of all marks across both papers are for quantitative skills (percentages, averages, totals, income calculations, constructing and interpreting graphs/data). Always show full working, not just a final answer -- AQA awards method marks that a bare correct answer alone will not earn.

Illustrative calculations in this course (e.g. income tax and National Insurance on a given gross pay, or a given CPI basket) use real UK institutions and a real current-style method, but tax bands, interest rates and similar figures change over time and are always given in the question in a real exam -- learn the method, not fixed numbers to memorise.
